learn.title: Data services, storage accounts and hosting choices for data
objectives: Describe storage account types and choose between Standard general-purpose v2 and the Premium account types.
Recognise storage account naming rules, service endpoints, encryption and secure transfer.
Tell structured, semi-structured and unstructured data apart.
Identify Azure data services: Azure SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, SQL Server on VMs, Azure Cosmos DB, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL.
Pick a suitable data hosting option from a scenario.
concepts: Storage account
A container that groups Azure Storage services (Blob, Files, Queue, Table) under one unique namespace, with shared settings such as performance, redundancy and access.
Standard general-purpose v2
The recommended account type for most scenarios. It supports Blob (including Data Lake Storage), Files, Queue and Table, and every redundancy option, including geo-redundancy.
Premium accounts
SSD-backed, low-latency accounts for one service each: Premium block blobs, Premium file shares or Premium page blobs. They don't offer geo-redundant options.
Account names
3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only, and globally unique across Azure, because the name becomes part of every endpoint URL.
Service endpoints
Each service has its own URL, for example https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net, plus file, queue, table and dfs (Data Lake Storage) endpoints.
Encryption and secure transfer
Azure Storage encrypts all data at rest by default. 'Secure transfer required' (on by default) rejects plain HTTP requests.
Access keys and SAS
Account keys give full access to the whole account. A shared access signature (SAS) grants limited, time-bound access to specific resources.
Structured, semi-structured, unstructured
Structured: fixed schema in rows and columns. Semi-structured: self-describing formats such as JSON or XML. Unstructured: files such as images, video and PDFs.
Relational databases in Azure

Azure SQL Database (PaaS), Azure SQL Managed Instance (PaaS with near-full SQL Server compatibility), SQL Server on Azure VMs (IaaS), and Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL (managed open-source engines).
Azure Cosmos DB
A fully managed, globally distributed NoSQL database with low latency, elastic scale, multi-region writes and several APIs (NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table, PostgreSQL).
comparisons: Standard: general-purpose, lower cost per GB, all redundancy options. Premium: SSD, low latency, high transaction rates, LRS or ZRS only.
SQL Database vs Managed Instance vs SQL on VMs

SQL Database: fully managed single databases or pools. Managed Instance: managed, near-full SQL Server instance features for lift-and-shift. SQL on VMs: full control of the OS and SQL Server, and you manage it.
Relational: fixed schema, joins and transactions. NoSQL (Cosmos DB): flexible schema, horizontal scale and global distribution.
Keys = full account access, so guard and rotate them. SAS = scoped permissions with an expiry time.
traps: Storage account names can't contain uppercase letters, hyphens or underscores.
Premium storage accounts don't offer GRS or GZRS. Geo-redundancy needs Standard general-purpose v2.
You can't switch an existing account between Standard and Premium; create a new account and copy the data.
Encryption at rest is on by default. You don't have to turn it on.
Cosmos DB is NoSQL. It's not a relational SQL Server service, despite its SQL-like query API.
SQL Server on Azure VMs is IaaS, so patching and backups stay your job unless you automate them.
revision: Name rules: 3–24, lowercase and numbers, globally unique.
Endpoints: blob, file, queue, table, dfs, with .core.windows.net.
Premium: block blobs (fast objects), file shares (fast SMB/NFS), page blobs (disk-like random I/O).
JSON = semi-structured; images and video = unstructured; tables = structured.
Need SQL Server instance features with no OS work: SQL Managed Instance. Need global NoSQL: Cosmos DB.
